title: Industry Growth and Political Spending: Research Plan
document_type: Research plan (Paul's own research note; specifies tests and sources, reports no estimated results)
coverage: Full text read in one pass: all 301 lines of the 29,981-character file (_text/46495cfa916e.txt), Sections 1-9. No annotation files exist (annot_sha12s is empty), so paul_markup is empty and nothing was dropped. p.note is true, so the author is treated as Paul. No ext/rel override files existed. Metadata hints verified: title, author, 2026 date and research-note venue are correct; the document is a plan, not a results paper.
research_question: Do industries spend differently on politics (federal campaign contributions and lobbying) when they have grown, are growing, or expect to grow? Does a published industry growth forecast predict subsequent spending, and do expectations about House and Senate control help explain spending?
theory: Better performance could supply more money for political spending; weak performance or a weak forecast could instead prompt spending to seek favorable policy. The sign of the relationship is to be estimated, not assumed.
data: Target panel of annual sector-year observations, 2008-2025, for nine sectors where comparable data exist: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance, auto manufacturing, crypto, Credit Arms, Fintech, Property and Casualty insurance, Telecom. Odd years retained; incomplete 2026 excluded. Unit is sector-year; spending in millions of 2025 dollars. Sources: IBISWorld revenue and archived forecasts; Mentat/FEC contributions split by job tier; Melange LDA and LobbyView lobbying; IEM congressional control forecasts; Minneapolis Fed CPI. Final N is not yet fixed: verified contribution years overlap the congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022. Strict annual growth inputs: 53 in the original collection, 86 in the expanded nine-sector grid.
method: Multiple linear regression by OLS with a separate intercept per sector (sector fixed effects). Contributions: Y_it = a_i + b X_it + c Pres_t + d Midterm_t + e ExpectedDemHouse_t + f ExpectedDemSenate_t + error. Lobbying adds CurrentDemHouse_t and CurrentDemSenate_t. X is prior actual growth, same-year actual growth, or predicted growth (tests C1-C3 and L1-L3). Growth in percentage points. Job-tier extension: pooled model with sector-by-tier baselines and growth x tier terms, Employee as reference. Chamber extension: linear model of Democratic share of contributions. Further extensions: prior and predicted growth together; year indicators in place of national controls; logged spending for positive observations. Simple regression only to illustrate scatterplots.
identification: No causal identification is claimed. Identifying variation is within-sector over time, after election-cycle and congressional-expectation controls. Predicted growth is taken from the latest IBISWorld report published by December 31 of the prior year, so it precedes the spending year. Congressional expectations are concurrent IEM averages and may not be known before all spending in a year. Results are framed as associations consistent with a response to public forecasts, not knowledge of firms' private expectations.
scope: US federal political spending by nine industry sectors, 2008-2025: candidate-committee contributions (personal versus organizational/PAC channels) and lobbying expenditures. Sector membership follows workbook rosters (40 company names) and industry proxies: Credit Arms is a proxy for workbook companies, Telecom is analyzed at component level, and Fintech lacks a comparable annual series. Life insurance and auto manufacturing are not among the published workbooks checked.

key_findings.finding: Design is OLS with sector fixed effects and six core tests: C1-C3 explain contributions and L1-L3 explain lobbying, each with prior actual, same-year actual, or predicted growth as the growth regressor.
key_findings.numbers: 6 core tests; growth in percentage points; spending in millions of 2025 dollars

key_findings.finding: Predicted growth must come from the latest IBISWorld report published by December 31 of year t-1 that forecasts year t, using numerator and denominator from the same vintage.
key_findings.location: Section 4, Predicting growth: preserve the original forecast date
key_findings.numbers: Example: report estimates 2019 revenue at 100 and 2020 at 105, giving 5 percent

key_findings.finding: Readiness check: verified contribution years overlap the prepared congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022, too little annual variation to identify the full control specification.
IBISWorld collection size: 63 original reports yielding 53 strict annual sector-year values; the expanded nine-sector grid has 86 strict annual revenue-growth inputs with explicit missing rows.
key_findings.numbers: 63 reports; 53 then 86 strict annual inputs; 12 supplemental observations kept separate

key_findings.finding: Banking and credit-union revenue include 2006, while life insurance and auto extracts start in 2007, leaving their 2008 lagged-growth observation incomplete.
key_findings.numbers: 2006 start for banks and credit unions; 2007 for life and auto

key_findings.finding: Crypto has only one verified original forecast: a Statista U.S. cryptocurrency-platform revenue forecast for 2025 of minus 3.78 percent, available by December 26, 2024, kept as a separate proxy.
Telecom is kept at component level (wireless and cable archives, 36 reports) because cable's revenue definition changes; Fintech has only dated multi-year projections and no comparable annual series.
key_findings.location: Section 6A, table rows for Telecom and Fintech

key_findings.finding: Congressional control forecasts (IEM) are available 2008-2022 only; 2023-2025 are missing, and the later election result must never substitute for a missing forecast.

Job-tier test uses a pooled model with sector-by-tier baselines and growth-by-tier interactions, Employee as reference; the existing Employee class includes unrecognized-title fallbacks that must be flagged.
key_findings.numbers: Chief slope term q; Middle Management slope term r

key_findings.finding: Partisan direction is tested with a per-chamber Democratic share outcome, D/(D+R), with zero denominators set to missing; party, presidential and other committee flows are not assigned to a chamber without a defensible mapping.

Lobbying outcome must keep expenses_total and income_total distinct, since client reports and outside-registrant receipts can refer to overlapping money; the four-sector LDA aggregate does not cover all nine sectors.
key_findings.numbers: 2 recorded measures analyzed separately; LDA annual rows 2021-2025 plus partial 2026

key_findings.finding: Inference caution: with few independent sector groups, ordinary independent-row OLS standard errors are not sufficient for strong significance claims, so repeated observations and small-sample uncertainty must be assessed.

measures: Dependent variables: annual federal candidate contributions (personal and organizational/PAC channels) and lobbying expenditures, in millions of inflation-adjusted 2025 dollars using annual CPI multiplier 321.9 over CPI. Independent variables: actual growth as 100 times (revenue ratio minus 1); prior-year growth; predicted growth from the report vintage; expected Democratic House and Senate control on a 0-1 scale (IEM, converted from Republican probability); current Democratic House and Senate control (1/0); presidential and midterm indicators. Job tiers: Chief, Middle Management, Employee. Partisan outcome: Democratic share of contributions per chamber.
limitations: Plan only: no estimated results are reported in the document.
Few independent sector groups (nine planned, fewer usable); ordinary OLS standard errors understate uncertainty; repeated observations must be accounted for.
Verified contribution years overlap congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022, so the full control specification is not yet identified.
IEM congressional forecasts are concurrent averages, not necessarily known before all spending in the year, and are missing for 2023-2025.
IBISWorld forecasts proxy public expectations only; they do not reveal private firm forecasts or whether a donor read the report.
Credit Arms is an industry proxy for workbook companies with OneMain and equipment-finance scope differences needing sensitivity checks.
Telecom is component-level; Fintech lacks a comparable annual series; crypto has one verified forecast.
Auto 2011-2012 uses a car and light-truck component reconstruction and needs a check excluding it; several forecast price bases differ and some values are inferred.
Chief classification uses a non-date-specific executive-name override; historical tier comparisons need role at donation date or a sensitivity test.
Employee tier includes unrecognized-title fallbacks; lobbying has no donor job-tier split in verified sources.
Lobbying: expenses_total and income_total measure overlapping money and cannot be simply added; older undifferentiated amount totals are not comparable without checking.
Historical contribution coverage before 2021 is not established in the local workbook extracts; FEC bulk data may be needed.
Sources cover only the selected sectors and are not an exhaustive archive of forecasts.
